analysis.one_liner: Locks in existing greenhouse gas emission standards for new cars through model year 2025, blocking EPA rollback.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee; no vote was ever held.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would put the force of law behind the Obama-era greenhouse gas emission standards for cars and light trucks, model years 2022 through 2025. It would stop the EPA from carrying out its April 2018 determination to reconsider and weaken those standards, which the bill's findings describe as an attack on the largest climate policy in effect at the time. The practical effect is that new vehicles would keep getting cleaner and more fuel-efficient, saving drivers money at the pump.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers, who would save on fuel because automakers must keep meeting the stricter efficiency standards, and everyone exposed to vehicle pollution, since less gasoline burned means less smog and fewer greenhouse gas emissions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Drivers and people breathing vehicle exhaust

how_it_helps.text: The bill gives legal force to the 2012 EPA rule setting greenhouse gas standards for vehicles model years 2017 through 2025 and to the January 2017 final determination keeping the 2022-2025 standards in place, overriding the EPA's April 2018 decision to reopen them [S3].
The bill states that cars and light trucks would continue to emit less carbon dioxide, cutting fuel costs for drivers and reducing pollution that harms air quality and public health [S3].

The bill bars the EPA from issuing any rule or taking any action that would effectively weaken the standards for model years 2022 through 2025, giving manufacturers and consumers regulatory certainty [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Automakers, which would have to keep meeting the stricter emission and efficiency targets rather than getting the loosened standards the EPA had proposed, and by extension the oil industry, which sells the gasoline that efficient vehicles burn less of.

drawbacks.text: Automakers argued the standards were too costly and pressed the administration to loosen them; keeping the stricter targets through 2025 could raise the price of new vehicles or squeeze manufacturers' profits, costs that could be passed to buyers.

The bill would lock the standards into federal statute, removing the EPA's normal ability to revisit them through the rulemaking process even if new evidence showed an adjustment was warranted; the standards' footprint-based design also gives smaller, more efficient vehicles stricter targets than larger ones, which some see as pressuring vehicle choices [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's main benefit to ordinary people is real but moderate: lower fuel bills and cleaner air over time. The main cost falls on automakers, whose own technical record — cited in the bill itself — indicated they could meet the standards at lower cost than previously estimated. The heavier drawback is procedural: writing the standards into law replaces the agencies' usual ability to update rules with new data, trading regulatory flexibility for certainty.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, where it sat with no hearings, no markup, and no vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Edward Markey introduced the bill on April 10, 2018, with six Democratic cosponsors, in direct response to the EPA's April 2, 2018 determination to reconsider the 2022-2025 vehicle emission standards [S5].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day [S5].
No further action was ever taken on the bill; it never received a hearing or a vote and died in committee when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the EPA's April 2018 determination stood, clearing the way for weaker vehicle emission standards. Automakers seeking looser targets and the oil industry, which sells the fuel efficient cars burn less of, came out ahead; drivers did not.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Automakers wanting looser rules and oil sellers

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to lock in the vehicle emission standards against the EPA's rollback

for.name: Sens. Whitehouse, Van Hollen, Smith, Blumenthal, Merkley, and Bennet

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill during the remainder of the 115th Congress

against.name: EPA Administrator Scott Pruitt
against.what_they_did: Issued the April 2018 determination reopening and weakening the basis for the 2022-2025 vehicle emission standards, the action the bill sought to override

sides.party_line_note: All seven sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican supported the bill, and the Republican-controlled committee never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would have forced manufacturers to keep meeting stricter emission and efficiency targets through model year 2025, raising compliance costs and limiting flexibility. Many automakers had pressed for looser rules, though the bill's own findings cite a technical record showing the standards were achievable at lower cost than estimated.

More fuel-efficient vehicles burn less gasoline, so keeping the stricter standards in place would reduce fuel sales. The industry's gain from the bill's failure was weaker efficiency rules for a decade of new vehicles.
